newsitem.title: DUBAI: Iraq's Gulf oil terminal comes under scrutiny.
newsitem.headline: Iraq's Gulf oil terminal comes under scrutiny.

text.p: Iraq's rebuilt Mina al Bakr oil export terminal has come under the close scrutiny of international firms planning to lift Iraqi crude under a resumed United Nations "oil-for-food" deal.

Gulf-based oil and shipping executives said on Monday that Mina al Bakr could cope with a major increase in Iraqi exports but they were concerned about the operational safety of the port which successfully handled an average of 270,000 barrels per day (bpd) in the first 180-day period of the U.N. deal.

"I'm sure they can meet the new target. The facilities have been repaired, the metering improved but safety worries linger," said a shipper with close knowledge of the deep-water terminal which has heavily damaged by allied forces in the 1991 Gulf War.
Disagreements between Baghdad and the U.N. over aid distribution has delayed the second 180-phase of the deal which was to have started in early June.

Now Baghdad, having come to an agreement over the distribution plan, is faced with having to more than double its exports to 1.5 million bpd to raise $1 billion before this stage of the plan expires on September 6.

But concerns remain over how the terminal, 12 miles (19 km) off the southern Fao Peninsula, will cope with an additional workload because of increased tanker traffic loading oil to markets mainly in the U.S. Gulf coast and the Far East.

"The port falls short of international standards. If there was any incident there is little effective oil spill or fire fighting equipment to react quickly enough," said one Gulf-based shipping manager.

Exports of Basrah Light crude from al Bakr are expected to accelerate well above the 270,000 bpd mark, putting additional strain on the terminal which Iraqi officials confidently say can handle more than 1.3 million bpd.

Customers in the first wave of exports from the terminal included U.S. majors, Japanese oil firms and Russian traders. Many of these, together with state-owned India Oil Corp, are expected to lift again when exports resume.
Shippers are also expecting high insurance premiums to take vessels to Mina al Bakr.

Tug boats, vital to berth and export large crude tankers, supplied by a private firm in the United Arab Emirates for the first phase of the deal have been withdrawn after disagreement over the contract, shippers said.

"There is a requirement from Iraq for support vessels but we're not going in unless there is a clear payment structure. Banks are not honouring (Iraqi) letters of credit," another shipper in the region said.
Iraq does have its own tugs though the number and condition of these and other support vessels is not known.
Mina al Bakr is also unlikely to be stretched above safety capacities as a twin pipeline linking Iraq's northern oilfields to Turkey's Mediterranean coast can handle 1.5 million bpd.
The line carried some 400,000 bpd in the first part of the U.N.-supervised program which ran from December 10, 1996 to June 7.
